title: Severe hyperkalemia
banner: DRAFT, NOT clinically reviewed. Fictional scenario specification; never imported, published or shown to learners.
learning_objectives: Recognise that a high potassium needs urgent assessment and cardiac monitoring.
Support the prescribed treatment steps without choosing drugs or doses.
Monitor glucose after insulin-glucose and potassium for rebound.
Know what is outside nursing scope.

sources.use: UKKA acute hyperkalaemia guideline, July 2026: hospital summary of recommendations and glucose-monitoring evidence read
FDA insulin label: hypoglycaemia, hypokalaemia, monitoring

required_sources: UKKA chapters on pseudohyperkalaemia, dialysis patients and potassium binders in full
Unit hyperkalaemia protocol and electrolyte replacement/removal policies
Reuse terms of the UKKA guideline (none stated in the text; no enquiry made)
gaps: No published clinical scenario may exist until the review phase: this is a specification only.
The branching content, consequences and scoring are the author's reading of the cited sources and have had no clinical review.
Calcium, insulin-glucose, salbutamol and binder doses, rates and preparations are in the guideline and are deliberately not reproduced; they come from orders and the unit protocol.
UK adult guideline with a review date of October 2026; critical-care alternatives (for example dialysis or bicarbonate) are medical decisions and not written.
The potassium and ECG thresholds are not used in the scenario's observations as bands.

AI source comparison 2026-11-16: UKKA 2026 detailed Guideline 14.1 (urgent 12-lead ECG at ≥6.0) and 14.2 (continuous monitoring at ≥6.5 or ECG changes) were checked. Delaying escalation to repeat a potassium of 6.8 with ECG changes was corrected from partial credit to zero. Full simulation branch and local protocol remain unreviewed by a credentialed clinician.
permissions: Cited sources are paraphrased only; see the licensing register for each source's reproduction status.
UKKA: no reuse statement found; verify.
setting: A fictional adult with acute kidney injury on a fictional unit.

steps.info: The laboratory reports a markedly raised potassium on a patient with acute kidney injury. The patient is quiet and the monitor shows tall, narrow T waves.

options.text: Assess immediately, call the responsible clinician urgently, obtain an urgent 12-lead ECG and ensure continuous ECG monitoring per the unit's emergency pathway.
options.feedback: UKKA July 2026 recommends urgent 12-lead ECG at K⁺ ≥6.0 mmol/L and continuous ECG monitoring at ≥6.5 mmol/L or with ECG changes. At 6.8 with ECG changes, prompt escalation and monitoring are indicated while the team confirms the result and directs treatment.
options.consequence: The doctor attends and a 12-lead ECG is arranged while monitoring continues.

options.text: Repeat the sample and tell the doctor only if the second result is also high.
options.feedback: At K⁺ 6.8 mmol/L with concerning ECG changes, urgent clinical assessment, a 12-lead ECG and continuous rhythm monitoring must proceed immediately. Repeat or point-of-care sampling may run in parallel if pseudohyperkalaemia is suspected; do not postpone escalation.
options.consequence: The patient is not assessed urgently while waiting for the repeat result; dangerous rhythm changes may progress.

options.text: Record the result and review it at the next round.
options.feedback: A markedly raised potassium needs urgent action, not routine review.
options.consequence: The patient's rhythm deteriorates before anyone acts.

steps.info: The doctor orders a stepwise treatment for the heart and for shifting potassium into cells, and asks you to get ready.

options.text: Prepare and give the prescribed treatments per the order and the unit protocol, with secure venous access and continuous ECG monitoring, and check the glucose before insulin-glucose is given.
options.feedback: The guideline describes a stepwise approach with cardiac monitoring and secure access and notes the pre-treatment glucose in preventing hypoglycaemia; the drugs and amounts come from the order and protocol.
options.consequence: Treatment is given safely and the glucose check is on the record.

options.text: Choose which treatments to give and work out the amounts yourself to save the doctor's time.
options.feedback: Choosing drugs and amounts is a prescriber and protocol decision.
options.consequence: A dosing error occurs and the incident has to be reported.

options.text: Skip the pre-treatment glucose check to start the insulin sooner.
options.feedback: The guideline links hypoglycaemia risk to the glucose before and after insulin-glucose, so the check is part of safe treatment.
options.consequence: The patient develops a low glucose that could have been anticipated.

steps.info: Treatment has been given and the monitor shows less ECG change.

options.text: Monitor the glucose at regular intervals for at least six hours after insulin-glucose, longer if the patient is at high risk, and follow the potassium results closely for a rebound, reporting any fall in glucose or rise in potassium.
options.feedback: The guideline recommends regular glucose checks for at least 6 hours after insulin-glucose, extended for high-risk patients, and close potassium monitoring for rebound after the first response.
options.consequence: A low glucose is caught early and a rebound is picked up.

options.text: Check the glucose once at the end of the shift.
options.feedback: Hypoglycaemia is most likely within the first hours after insulin-glucose, so checks must be regular.
options.consequence: A low glucose goes unnoticed for hours.

options.text: Stop the extra monitoring once the potassium has fallen.
options.feedback: The effect can wear off and rebound hyperkalaemia can follow, so monitoring continues.
options.consequence: The potassium rises again and is found late.

learning_points: A markedly raised potassium needs urgent assessment, ECG changes check and continuous cardiac monitoring.
Treatment drugs and amounts are prescriber and protocol decisions; the nurse prepares, gives per order and monitors.
Monitor glucose regularly after insulin-glucose and potassium for rebound.
